data.title: Palm oil stocks slide after Singapore begins looking into which firms responsible for haze
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Shares of palm oil producers fell on Friday (Oct 16) after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the country is looking into which companies may be responsible for haze-causing fires.

Where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries, said PM Wong in a Facebook post on Thursday.

First Resources shares fell as much as 9.1 per cent to S$3.71 at 9.20 am. The counter pared some losses to end the day 6.9 per cent lower at S$3.80.

Bumitama Agri retreated 7.5 per cent to an intraday low of S$1.73, then rebounded somewhat to close 4.8 per cent lower at S$1.78. Golden Agri-Resources dropped as much as 3.4 per cent to S$0.28.

The Straits Times reported on Thursday that a recent Greenpeace investigation had named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points.

First Resources on Thursday defended itself, stating that fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. It attributed the elevated fire risk in West Kalimantan to a “severe” El Nino-induced drought. Indonesia on Thursday blamed peatland degradation by past food estates for its worst wildfire season in 11 years, and said it will work to restore its peat ecosystem.

Air quality deteriorated across all of Singapore overnight. The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index reading in the central region hit the “very unhealthy” level at midnight on Friday and stood at 227 at 9 am – a new high for the year. Readings in the rest of the country were at the “unhealthy” level.

Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu on Wednesday said that Singapore was “keeping its options open” on whether it will take action against errant companies under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.

That followed a National Environment Agency spokesperson saying that the agency “has been closely monitoring the haze situation, gathering information on fire hot spots, their sources and impact on Singapore’s air quality”.

data.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill to lawmakers
data.description:
[SAN FRANCISCO] Anthropic has presented its own draft bill to US lawmakers with a plan for regulating artificial intelligence safety and security, in a moment of heightened concern about the potential risks of the rapidly advancing technology.  

The proposal suggests the government could block the release of an AI model if it’s determined to imminently risk killing or injuring more than 50 people or causing more than US$1 billion in damages, according to Politico, which first reported on the bill.

The threat must be a result of the model creating or releasing a biological weapon, the AI going beyond human control, or a cyberattack, Politico reported. 

“This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” a company spokesperson said.

The bill would mandate that AI makers must test their models and share findings with the public; it also would require AI companies to allow independent evaluators to routinely review models, the spokesperson said.

“Our proposal also grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models,” the spokesperson said. “These are sensible policies we believe Congress should act on.”

The company declined to comment on how broadly it has pitched the proposal and how it’s been received so far.

In recent months, a series of breaches and hacks led by AI models have fuelled anxiety over the technology’s potentially catastrophic risks, spurring calls from Washington to Silicon Valley for new safeguards, but so far, US President Donald Trump’s administration has rejected calls for more oversight. BLOOMBERG

data.title: US posts US$1.99 trillion budget gap for 2026 on spending rise
data.description:
[WASHINGTON, DC] The US federal budget deficit widened to nearly US$2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, serving as a fresh reminder of the scale of government borrowing needs and leaving the nation on track for a record-high debt burden in coming years.

For the fiscal year through September, the deficit widened to US$1.99 trillion, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday (Oct 16). That marks about a 12 per cent increase on the US$1.78 trillion gap recorded for last year. Spending rose by about 6 per cent, to US$7.4 trillion, while receipts increased roughly 3 per cent, to US$5.4 trillion.

This year’s jump in US Treasury yields, along with the ever-growing base of government debt, made interest payments a key contributor to the widening deficit for 2026. Net interest climbed by US$81.4 billion, to total a record US$1.05 trillion.

Debt-servicing costs are one of the top three expenses for the government. Social Security is the biggest item, with outlays on that entitlement program rising by US$86.4 billion for the fiscal year, to US$1.67 trillion. Medicare spending climbed US$76 billion, to US$1.07 trillion.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has singled out tariff refunds as a key to the wider deficit, after he touted a narrowing in the gap for 2025.

Those payments were tied to the Supreme Court’s February ruling invalidating the bulk of US President Donald Trump’s tariff hikes in his second term. The administration is in the process of constructing a fresh tariff wall via other legislation.

Outsize deficit

This year marks the fourth straight with a deficit roughly around US$2 trillion. The figures suggest the gap was roughly 6 per cent of gross domestic product – an unusually high figure at a time of relatively low unemployment.

Officially, the gap narrowed last year, though that was thanks to an accounting measure – the 2025 Republican tax act tightened limits on student loans, and the Treasury booked that as a reduction in 2025 spending.

While Bessent has declared that the US can bend the debt curve down quickly – thanks especially to a faster sustained economic growth rate as the artificial intelligence boom spurs American productivity – many economists, investors and even other senior public officials are sceptical.

International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said Oct 14 that “growth, of course, helps but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments”. A counselor to Bessent, the recently appointed David Zervos, took issue with the assessment, saying in comments to CNBC that IMF has had “messy” forecasts in the past.

Georgieva’s predecessor, current European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde, said the same day that the US deficit “needs to be tackled by any country that is, you know, in that particular category”. Congressional Budget Office (CBO) director Phillip Swagel said on Oct 8 that it wasn’t “plausible” for growth alone to stabilise US debt levels.

The nonpartisan CBO warned in February that US debt as a ratio of gross domestic product was on track to surpass the 106 per cent record set in 1946, just after World War II, by 2030. One gauge of US public debt outstanding surpassed a record US$40 trillion last month.

Bessent has vowed to put forward a fiscal consolidation plan, potentially during the lame duck session of Congress if Republicans lose control of either the House or Senate. 

Yet in the meantime, Trump keeps suggesting more outlays. He has called for a close to US$500 billion increase in defence spending and has also promised US$5,000 checks to every American if Republicans maintain control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections next month.

For the month of September, the US spent US$27 billion more than it brought in revenue.

Trump’s tax cut package of 2025 has also had an impact on the deficit. While revenue collected from individual taxes in 2026 increased by US$189 billion, corporate income taxes collection fell by more than US$70 billion after the Trump administration’s signature 2025 tax bill extended many tax cuts and introduced new deductions for corporations. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries rise from almost 1-year low
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Foreign holdings of US Treasuries rose in August from the lowest level since October 2025, led by increases in the stockpiles of Canada and Belgium.

Overseas holdings climbed more than US$83 billion from July, according to data published by the Treasury Department on Friday (Oct 16). The total now stands at US$9.33 trillion. 

The foreign holdings data incorporate changes in valuation as well as net sales and purchases. The Bloomberg US Treasury index advanced 0.3 per cent in August, before a tumble in September on concerns about persistent inflation and a new cycle of Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes.

Japan, the biggest foreign holder of Treasuries, saw a US$36 billion drop in its holdings, to US$1.1 trillion, the lowest since December 2024.

Japanese officials were intervening over the summer in the foreign-exchange market, buying yen amid a slump in the currency to its weakest in four decades against the dollar. Japanese data last month suggested Tokyo sold a portion of its holdings of Treasuries and other securities.

Mainland China, the third-largest holder of Treasuries, saw a US$27 billion fall in August, Friday’s report showed. The total is now at an 18-year low of US$591 billion. Some analysts have said that Beijing might have channelled some of its transactions in US securities via other nations, including Canada. 

Canada’s holding increased by US$38 billion to almost US$465 billion, while Belgium’s added nearly US$20 billion to about US$491 billion. 

The UK, the second-biggest holder of Treasuries, saw an US$11 billion increase in August, to surpass US$1 trillion for the first time. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Big US bank stocks log worst weekly losing streak since 2008
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Big US bank shares recorded their worst weekly losing streak since the 2008 Global Financial Crisis after quarterly earnings didn’t do enough to lift sentiment for the ailing sector.

The 24-member KBW Bank Index fell nearly 1 per cent this week and is well into correction territory, losing about 13 per cent since its last record in August. While the group has suffered larger sell-offs over the years – including an almost 17 per cent drawdown early this year – its six-week long decline would mark the longest such losing streak since 2008. 

Citigroup, State Street, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley are among the worst performers on the gauge. While, JPMorgan Chase is up about 2 per cent for the week.

Even before mixed quarterly earnings this week, the sector has been battered by worries around how artificial intelligence technology will disrupt the financial services space. A hot inflation print this week also added to concerns on how aggressive the Federal Reserve will be in its campaign to rein in persistent inflation.

“Big-bank stocks are facing a confluence of concerns, with a higher-for-longer rate backdrop raising the risk of slower economic growth and higher loan losses,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan.

“Third-quarter results did little to reverse the weakness, with stable operating leverage but mixed trading as fixed-income results disappointed despite strength in equities.” 

Sustained weakness in bank stocks can be a troubling sign for the economy, given the role lenders play in fuelling growth by providing credit.

The “rising funding costs for artificial intelligence companies are now adding questions about the durability of the capital-markets revenue opportunity tied to the infrastructure buildout,” said Chan. “Agentic AI is also emerging as a potential longer-term threat to the stable, low-cost deposits that drive bank profitability.”

The gauge has underperformed the S&P 500 Index in 18 of 21 trading days since the Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Sep 16, Barclays analyst Jason Goldberg wrote in an Oct 14 note. That’s unprecedented across rolling 21-session periods since the index’s May 1992 inception, he said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Apple says iPhone Duo demand extraordinary after delivery delays
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Apple said demand for the new iPhone Duo has been “nothing short of extraordinary” after shipping estimates slipped to the end of January of next year just minutes after pre-orders opened on Friday (Oct 16).

“The pre-order demand for iPhone Duo, our first foldable iPhone, has been nothing short of extraordinary. We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online,” the company said in a statement.

“Our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores worldwide to experience the iPhone Duo and the incredible full iPhone line-up for themselves,” it added, without disclosing whether inventory would be available for customers who were unable to secure pre-orders when the device goes on sale Oct 23.

Many customers who opened Apple’s online store Friday morning immediately encountered shipping delays stretching into November. Within minutes, delivery estimates slipped to December and then as far out as the end of January. The delays affect both colours and all storage configurations, ranging from 256 gigabytes to 2 terabytes.

For Apple, the iPhone Duo is one of the first major product debuts under new CEO John Ternus, who took the helm in September amid a flurry of announcements that has included the HomeView smart home hub and AirPods 5. Apple will introduce a touch-screen MacBook Pro and other devices later this month, Bloomberg reported.

Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Anurag Rana and Josh Christensen said in a note Friday that iPhone Duo sales could exceed their earlier estimates of 14 million units and US$28 billion in sales for the company’s fiscal 2027 year.

If Apple can persuade current Pro and Pro Max owners to switch to the base version of the foldable, they added, that would push up the iPhone’s average selling price by 82 per cent and 67 per cent, respectively.

Shares of Apple closed up 0.4 per cent to US$343.46 on Friday.

Compared with the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September, which went smoothly for customers who placed a timely order, securing an iPhone Duo was significantly more difficult. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Good Class Bungalow market activity picks up pace on ârealisticâ pricing
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] For most of this year, the well-heeled shopping for a bungalow in one of Singapore’s Good Class Bungalow (GCB) Areas have been able to take their time before deciding on which best suits their requirements.

That’s in contrast with a bullish market, where buyers must often decide quickly as their shortlisted properties may change hands before they can put in an offer, observes Steve Tay, executive director of Steve Tay Real Estate (STRE).

Most market watchers found the GCB market quieter in the first eight months of 2026, as buyers became more selective and sought greater value in the face of global geopolitical uncertainty, oil supply chain disruptions and other drags on sentiment.

Meanwhile, GCB owners with strong holding power continue to hang on to lofty price expectations significantly above market value. The widening buyer-seller price gap has contributed to a drop in transaction volumes and values.

As transacted prices come off the highs seen in the last two years – especially in the case of land with potential for redevelopment – some owners have withdrawn listings, market watchers say.

There have also not been many new listings.

But the market looks set to pick up in the final months of 2026, with momentum carrying over into the next year as well.

Lower sales activity

Bungalows in Singapore’s 39 GCB Areas (GCBAs) are the most exclusive form of landed housing on the island, with only about 2,700 such properties, according to market estimates.

These bungalows are nestled mostly in wooded areas on large plots in prime districts 10 (such as Nassim Road, Cluny Hill, Dalvey Road, Victoria Park Close and Queen Astrid Park) and 11 (such as Bukit Tunggal and Eng Neo Avenue).

There are also a few GCB Areas in districts 20 (Windsor Park), 21 (Kilburn Estate including Yarwood Avenue, and King Albert Park) and 23 (Chestnut Avenue).

Bungalows in GCBAs are subject to strict planning conditions to preserve their exclusivity and low-rise character.

A minimum plot size of 1,400 square metres or 15,070 square feet (sq ft) is the specified planning norm for newly created bungalows in GCBAs.

Property consultancy Knight Frank’s analysis of caveats on the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) Realis portal found 14 transactions in GCBAs, to the tune of S$406.2 million, in the first eight months of 2026. This is down from 17 deals worth S$530.6 million in the same period a year earlier.

Recent deals have brought this year’s caveated transactions to 17 as at Tuesday (Oct 13), with a total value of S$517.5 million. The latest sale was dated Sep 30.

Market watchers additionally estimate that at least S$800 million of deals have been contracted in the year to date where buyers did not lodge caveats.

In comparison, in 2025, there were 30 deals in GCBAs amounting to S$1 billion for which buyers lodged caveats. In addition, there were at least S$1 billion of non-caveated transactions, based on market estimates.

Some of last year’s non-caveated deals include properties in Cluny Hill (at S$85 million and S$52 million), Dalvey Road (S$61 million), Tanglin Hill (S$76 million), Cornwall Gardens (S$75 million) and Victoria Park Close (S$52 million and S$63 million).

The pool of caveated and non-caveated deals this year includes a vacant plot in Nassim Road, sold by former Sincere Watch boss Tay Liam Wee for S$92 million, as well as an old house in Bishopsgate, sold for S$40 million by four members of the founding family of traditional Chinese medicine group Eu Yan Sang.

More recently, an old house in Dalvey Road went for S$56 million or S$3,029 per square foot (psf) on site area.

It is being sold by Dr Goh Kia Seng, president of the Academy of Chinese Medicine, Singapore and chairman of Singapore Chung Hwa Medical Institution’s board.

The rich show restraint

Some agents in the luxury residential property market suggest that the slower GCB market may be due in part to a smaller number of top-tier ultra-high net worth (UHNW) individuals among newly minted Singapore citizens.

In general, only Singapore citizens can buy a landed property in a GCBA.

Boutique property consultancy firm JQT Private’s executive director Jacqueline Wong says: “It appears that the government has tightened the criteria for granting new citizenships, even when it comes to billionaires.”

This can weigh on GCB demand – especially for brand-new properties with bigger price quantums, as new citizens form the bulk of the buyer pool in this segment, market watchers note.

Nine in 10 UHNW new citizens want to buy a GCB, says Wong.

Such a property can be “a prized possession they look forward to acquiring after having made the journey” to becoming Singaporean.

“That’s why newly minted Singapore citizens are willing to pay a premium for the best-in-grade GCBs,” she adds. They find a GCB attractive because it offers “unparalleled privacy” and has a much bigger usable or built-up area than most penthouses.

A luxury residential agent who declined to be named points to another recent dampener on GCB demand: Beijing’s recent clampdown on offshore trusts, which has caused some UHNW Singapore citizens originally from China to take a pause before buying any big-ticket assets outside of China.

Over the years, observers have noted that some UHNW families structure GCB acquisitions using trusts – such as purchasing in trust for Singaporean minor children or establishing family trusts – to facilitate long-term wealth transfer and estate planning.

But in late July, Beijing imposed a 20 per cent income tax on the offshore trusts that could be seen as a grey area for UHNW individuals to harbour wealth.

Stepped-up enforcement of taxes on Chinese tax residents’ offshore income and gains have also stoked concern that the authorities could enlarge their tax dragnet and deter investment, as The Business Times reported in September.

“A lot of our clients are going through with their lawyers and bankers to see how they are going to be affected,” says the luxury residential agent who declined to be named.

“Before all this becomes very clear, they may want to stay out of big transactions.”

Tale of two sellers

Another major reason for the slower pace of GCB deals so far is owners sticking to unrealistic price expectations.

As Realstar Premier managing director Julian Yip notes: “Compared with those who own smaller landed homes, GCB sellers usually have better holding power. Unless the price is right, they will usually prefer to hold on to their property.”

That said, Yip highlights another group of owners “who prefer to rightsize their homes due to a change in their family demographic – and who will price their property more realistically”.

This group comprises silver-generation empty-nesters who opt to move into a smaller, more manageable home and free up more cash for retirement. Higher residential property taxes may provide additional motivation to part with a GCB that they don’t need.

“This profile of GCB sellers surfaced gradually in 2023, when the government began increasing the upper tiers of residential property tax rates, and has featured more strongly since 2025,” says Yip.

Such motivated sellers have realistic price expectations – and they are being greeted by enthusiastic buyers.

Tay of STRE notes that this is particularly so for sites with ageing bungalows that are ripe for redevelopment, as well as for older bungalows that are well maintained and need only minor renovations.

An old property in Jalan Sampurna, in the Oei Tiong Ham Park GCBA, recently went for at S$31.3 million or S$2,089 psf on land area – down from the S$42.8 million guide price when the site was marketed in March 2025.

In June this year, a pair of old freehold bungalows in Belmont Road sold for a total of S$60 million or about S$1,437 psf on the land area of 41,741 sq ft.

This was below the indicative price of S$88.8 million or S$2,128 psf, during an expression of interest exercise that closed in March 2025.

These transaction prices take into account features that may weigh on buyers, such as a retaining wall, a downward slope, or a site that is below road level or affected by a drainage reserve.

With transaction volumes lower, sellers are realising that buyers are “willing to wait and look around for more suitable options rather than chase prices up”, Tay notes.

“If sellers are willing to be reasonable on pricing, in line with fair market value, it is likely the property will find a buyer,” he adds.

Tay also highlights strong demand for brand-new, well-built GCBs with modern designs – a segment sought after for its scarcity.

“There is a pool of buyers who do not want to go through the hassle of two to three years of constructing their own home,” he says.

“These buyers are willing to pay a reasonable premium for the convenience of acquiring such a property that meets their requirement and that they can move into soon.”

Room for growth

Knight Frank Singapore research head Leonard Tay says that GCB demand this year has been “stable but selective”.

“While capital is still available, buyers appear to be more disciplined, placing a greater emphasis on underlying land value, with more focus on a site’s attributes and its redevelopment potential, and the long-term upside,” he adds.

He remarks that demand continues to be supported by potential buyers’ stock market and business gains, as well as “wealth inflows into Singapore” from some new citizens.

In recent months, STRE’s Tay has observed an increase in enquiries and viewing requests compared with the first two quarters.

“The catalysts for this are the more realistic pricing for the GCBs on sale, as well as potential buyers who have done well in their investments in financial markets and commodities,” he says.

Would-be buyers may include the owners of businesses in growth sectors such as semiconductor manufacturing and healthcare, who are now “taking some profits and parking them into a GCB for long-term wealth preservation”, he adds.

Looking ahead to 2027, Realstar’s Yip identifies two bright spots for the GCB market: Singapore’s immigration policy and the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP).

The Singapore government expects to take in around 25,000 to 30,000 new citizens annually over the next five years.

“Just 10 per cent of this number will equate to 2,500 new buyers of landed properties,” says Yip.

Meanwhile, the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s S$6.5 billion EQDP, first announced in 2025, is part of broader efforts to deepen investment capabilities, attract more capital into Singapore equities and boost investor participation.

Should more business owners opt for initial public offerings, founders and other existing shareholders would have an avenue to realise part of their investments.

Such liquidity could subsequently be deployed into other assets – including GCBs.

Knight Frank’s Tay notes that activity such as listings and asset divestments “can typically provide the capital that fuels demand for trophy residential assets among local business leaders”.

“Timely opportunity”

Both Knight Frank and Realstar project a 3 to 5 per cent increase in GCB prices in 2027. Knight Frank predicts that the volume of deals in GCBAs could be slightly higher year on year, while Realstar says the volume might be lower if geopolitical conflicts worsen.

Yip adds that the performance of the artificial intelligence sector and stock market, as well as economic and geopolitical stability, will affect sentiment in the GCB market in the near to medium term.

For instance, businesses in sectors such as semiconductors, data centres, or even construction could be hit if the much-feared AI bubble manifests and the industry crashes. “In turn, this may delay the plans of these business owners to buy a GCB.”

Still, predicting that transaction prices “will continue to go north” on a psf basis, Yip says: “There is potential of record-breaking sales.”

He tips top-tier locations, such as Nassim, Cluny, Dalvey, White House Park, Tanglin and Chatsworth, as areas to watch.

Yip expects that the transacted price gap between GCBs in the best locations and less prime areas – which has widened this year – will increase further in 2027, so “owners of properties in less prime areas might need to price them more realistically”.

At the same time, STRE’s Tay notes that “present pricing is at more realistic levels” than before.

“The current window presents a timely opportunity for GCB buyers to acquire good properties at fair values.”

Knight Frank’s Tay opines that beyond the existing bungalow on a site, prospective buyers should consider how land specifications lend to quality and long-term value, since “a house can be rebuilt”.

“Buyers should pay close attention to factors such as the plot shape and gradient, road frontage, planning parameters and future use.”

Finally, Wong of JQT suggests to clients that all those who will be living in the house visit a potential GCB home in person “to see if they like the vibes, the energy of the place”, rather than merely viewing it online.

Before making a decision, the multimillion-dollar question must be: “Do they feel a sense of peace in the various parts of the property?”

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CapitaLand India Trust, First Resources
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 16):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : Passenger traffic rose 2.8 per cent year on year in September, supported by healthy demand across most regions, it said on Thursday. The group said it carried 3.5 million passengers during the month, up 3.7 per cent from a year earlier. Shares of SIA closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.05 lower at S$6.49 on Thursday, before the news.

CapitaLand India Trust (Clint) : The trust on Thursday announced the launch of a new data centre in Chennai with an investment of about 19.4 billion rupees (US$203.2 million). CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai 01, Clint’s first data-centre development in the state of Tamil Nadu, will have a gross power capacity of 53 megawatts when completed by the end of 2026. Units of Clint fell 1.1 per cent or S$0.01 to S$0.88 on Thursday, before the news.

First Resources : The Singapore-listed palm oil producer on Thursday said fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. The response follows a report by The Straits Times citing a recent Greenpeace investigation, which named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points. Shares of First Resources fell 3.3 per cent or S$0.14 to S$4.08 on Thursday, before the filing.

data.title: Issue 216: Singaporeâs multi-fuel bunkering bet; listed companies hazy on haze risk
data.description:
Energy transition

Managing the transition to a multi-fuel bunkering future

As Singapore plans for a multi-fuel future for the maritime sector, its challenge is to be both versatile and efficient so that it can defend its status as a bunkering hub in the coming decades.

That means building up capabilities for different fuels while investing strategically to ensure that supply and demand are closely matched.

Singapore Senior Minister of State for Transport Murali Pillai says that the country is exploring the use of liquefied biomethane as a marine fuel, alongside plans to conduct its first ethanol bunkering operation and the release of guidelines for ammonia bunkering. Singapore is also expanding capacity for liquefied natural gas (LNG).

One of the maritime industry’s biggest decarbonisation challenges is how to replace the fossil-based marine fuel that powers vessels with greener alternatives. LNG, ethanol, methanol, methane and ammonia are among the leading candidates, while old classics like wind have also been incorporated into some modern designs.

Murali’s declarations, made at the Singapore International Bunkering Conference, reflect a bet that there will not be a single winner out of those alternatives.

Indeed, a recent analysis by the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) – an international think tank based in Singapore with funding support from industry and the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore – looks at different scenarios for the maritime fuel transition and none of them lead to a single dominant fuel by 2050.

“The future fuel landscape remains fragmented across all fuel types and in bunkering locations,” GCMD says in its report. “Shipowners that lock into a single fuel pathway today risk assets stranded by regulatory or cost outcomes.”

GCMD identifies four key signposts that affect uptake of alternative fuels:

The levelised cost of hydrogen is a primary determinant of the cost for low-carbon methanol and ammonia;

The cost of carbon dioxide obtained from biomass, which affects the cost of bio-methanol;

The cost trajectory of bio-methanol, which can be used in the near term and provide a bridge to greener electro-methanol in the longer term. Electro-methanol is produced using green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide.

Regulatory treatment of ethanol in fuels based on food crops, which has a “binary” impact on ethanol’s penetration in marine fuels.

The cost and carbon footprint of the different fuels also varies depending on available resources, which can vary by region. GCMD expects that bio-methanol will be “cheapest along global sea lanes, with Asia being the most cost-competitive”.

Ammonia bunkering will be more likely along Asia sea lanes due to low production costs in China and India, while bio-ethanol will be linked to US supply chains due to low American production costs.

Because there is so much uncertainty around those factors right now, ship owners are increasingly ordering dual-fuel vessels that can use existing marine fuels as well as one of the alternatives. However, since there is no single dual-fuel combination dominating the orders, different fuel mixes will likely be required for many years after these vessels are built.

Data compiled by the World Shipping Council shows that 94 per cent of vehicle carrier orders and 78 per cent of container ship orders by deadweight tonnage are for dual-fuel ships as of March 2026. There were 440 dual-fuel vehicle carriers and container ships on the water at the time of the data, and 764 on order.

Most of the dual-fuel container vessels on order are for conventional-and-methane and conventional-and-methanol engines. There is one container ship on order with ammonia capability.

It’s not hard to see why Singapore is taking a multi-fuel approach under these circumstances. If Singapore is to remain a bunkering hub, it will need to cater for the different potential fuel types in the pipeline.

But actually building the infrastructure and supply chains to provide multiple fuels can be costly, which makes it important to time investments and expenditures to match demand. At the moment, the vast majority of dual-fuel engines are still running on conventional fuel.

GCMD explains that conventional fuel is still significantly cheaper than low-carbon alternatives at the moment, which means that most dual-fuel vessels are still not switching.

The economics could change and green alternatives could become cost-competitive if emissions were taxed aggressively enough, GCMD says. The maritime sector is considering the possibility of imposing a US$700 per tonne of greenhouse gas emissions penalty under a proposed net zero framework, but international consensus is missing. The industry could make a decision in December at a meeting of the Marine Environment Protection Committee.

Amid that uncertainty, being too aggressive on building out infrastructure for alternative fuels when demand is still absent might make it difficult to recover costs, which would make it more difficult to maintain a commercially sustainable bunkering hub.

Singapore manages that risk by focusing on capability building for now. For instance, Singapore has developed a technical reference for ammonia bunkering, and is carrying out pilot bunkering trials for different fuels. The aim is to start building the software now to shorten the time to delivery when the need arises.

The economic and logistical realities of producing low-carbon fuel for ships means that green bunkering in the future will comprise a more heterogeneous landscape than the conventional marine fuel system we have today. But knowing what the end state might look like is only one part of the challenge; navigating the transition is the other, just as important part.

Climate risk

Risk disclosures on haze need more visibility

Singapore-listed companies may need to give more deliberate consideration to the haze as a risk to be managed, and assure investors of those considerations.

The prolonged season of the transboundary air pollution currently besieging Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia has disrupted a swathe of activities. For example, the haze has led to severe curtailment of outdoor activities and suspended flights.

Of course, this is not the first time that South-east Asia has encountered the haze, with the severe outbreak in 2013 leading to the enactment of Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. In fact, Singapore is so familiar with the haze that it has well-established guidelines on when pollution levels are unhealthy and the appropriate health and safety responses at those levels.

Yet many listed companies’ disclosures do not seem to directly address the risk posed by the haze, even for companies that would seem to be more exposed to such risk.

For instance, theme park developer Sim Leisure Group’s sustainability report identifies extreme weather as a material physical climate risk, but only considers that risk in the form of extreme rainfall and increased flooding. The bulk of the company’s revenues are from Malaysia and Singapore, where haze conditions pose an ongoing threat to guest numbers as well as worker health and safety at its outdoor theme parks.

ISOTeam, a building maintenance and estate upgrading group with a leading presence in building painting works, performs substantial work outdoors. Its climate-related disclosures discuss heatwaves, water stress and sea level rise as key physical climate risks. There is no mention of the haze.

Investors might be concerned that a company deems sea level rise, which may only manifest at a serious enough level many years into the future, important enough to disclose but not the haze, which occurs almost every year at varying levels of severity.

This is not to suggest that companies have not been dealing with the haze. In fact, both of the mentioned companies have been around long enough to be familiar with serious haze events of past years.

But leaving the haze out of disclosures can create a gap in investors’ appreciation of how a company manages climate risk, and raise questions about the thoroughness of a company’s assessment of climate risks. This is increasingly relevant with rising temperatures expected to raise the severity and frequency of serious haze events, even if human activities are still a major underlying cause of the haze.

The haze is also a reminder that companies need to be especially conscientious when it comes to assessing their exposure to climate risk, and not overly rely on convenient boilerplate risks. One of the biggest dangers of climate change is unpredictability, so prudent companies should be assessing the exposure of various aspects of their businesses in detail.

data.title: Chinese stocks turn biggest losers as global AI trade stumbles
data.description:
[BEIJING] Chinese firms have emerged as the biggest losers of the faltering global artificial intelligence trade, a setback for Beijing’s efforts to use stock markets to supercharge its ambition of technological supremacy.

The Nasdaq-style Star50 Index has tumbled nearly 40 per cent in the current half year, becoming the world’s worst-performing major tech gauge. Major chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits Shanghai and Moore Threads Technology have both shed around half of their value during this period. 

The ChiNext index, similarly focused on hardware stocks, has lost 36 per cent. 

It marks a reversal of fortunes from earlier this year, when the Star50 enjoyed a stunning rally as investors ignored frothy valuations to bet on Beijing’s policy push and ride the global AI boom.

All that enthusiasm has since unravelled as scrutiny of future demand and earnings prospects hit Chinese stocks the hardest, a worrisome development given the heavier reliance on equity financing by the country’s firms.

“It would be much harder for China to achieve its AI ambitions if technology stocks remain under pressure for an extended period,” said Leonid Mironov, a portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital. “If the weakness goes on for more than six months, this will make fundraising difficult and also imply that the market is unimpressed with the technological progress being achieved.”

The Star50 surged around 75 per cent between April and June – beating Korea’s Kospi – on optimism about Chinese firms’ technological breakthroughs and strong state support. The gauge traded at over 80 times forward earnings at its peak on Jun 30. Yet as sentiment abruptly turned, the sector’s high valuations have become a liability. 

“The global AI-hardware sell-off, spanning the Nasdaq and Korea, hit China A-shares hardest after foreign investors crowded into the sector in Q2,” Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Jason Liao and Marvin Chen wrote in a note, referring to China’s onshore equities. 

Outflows from a trading link with Hong Kong that allows foreign investors access to Chinese local stocks totalled an estimated 90 billion yuan (US$13.5 billion) in the third quarter, the biggest in a year and reversing more than half of the inflows between April and June, the note said.

The recent sell-off has also weighed on some of China’s hottest trading debuts. Memory-chip giant CXMT, which went public in July, has fallen 27 per cent from its post-listing peak. Similarly, robotics firm Yushu Technology, has lost around 50 per cent from an August high shortly after its initial public offering.

Chinese companies have fetched a combined US$37 billion from onshore IPOs this year, lifting annual proceeds to their highest in three years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Tech firms accounted for over a third of the funds raised.

The underperformance of China’s tech stocks poses a challenge for authorities that are keen to use capital markets to fuel the firms’ growth. The country’s AI-linked national champions and startups have shown a stronger preference for equity financing over debt, partly reflecting the higher costs for them to issue bonds globally. 

Equities are “the default source” of funding for China’s AI firms, according to Mironov.

“If the slump is prolonged it will have an impact and Beijing may need to be more proactive in expediting financial sector reforms and potentially deploying the national team more aggressively,” he said, referring to a group of state-backed funds used by regulators to stabilise markets.

To be sure, the tide may shift if the government significantly increases efforts to prop up the languishing market. Financial regulators held a meeting Thursday (Oct 15) to discuss stabilisation measures and called on the national team to accelerate stock purchases. Any pleasant surprises from the upcoming third-quarter earnings season may also help brighten the mood. 

Still, some investors are sceptical about the outlook because China’s AI-related stocks remain expensive even after the recent sell-off. The Star50 now trades at over 40 times forward earnings. It compares with less than five times for South Korea’s Kospi and 21 times for the Nasdaq 100.

“Current levels represent a technical pullback, not a value play,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at Gam Investment Management. “For many high-potential tech names, big bargains won’t appear until they fall another 30 to 50 per cent.” BLOOMBERG
